title: NASA’s new dark energy space telescope can also detect killer asteroids
gist: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launching from Kennedy Space Center at the end of August to study dark matter and dark energy, is being repositioned by researchers as a planetary-defense asset after the Trump administration threatened it with funding cuts. Its 300-megapixel infrared camera covers a field roughly 100 times larger than Hubble, letting it refine hazardous-asteroid orbits by orders of magnitude in days and triage which objects deserve scarce JWST follow-up time.

insights.claim: The planetary-defense case for the Roman telescope was deliberately constructed after the mission was again threatened with significant funding cuts by the Trump administration, making the science pitch an explicit political survival strategy.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Science programs are now marketing dual-use defense value to survive appropriations — expect more missions to reframe around planetary defense or national security.
insights.quote: My colleague Rick Cosentino [a planetary scientist at NASA] said to me in July 2025 that we need to show what Roman can do for planetary defense as a way to further increase the visibility of the mission with lawmakers and taxpayers,

insights.claim: The repositioning is being executed through a formal multi-institutional proposal presented at the Europlanet Science Congress at The Hague in September, showing the campaign runs through peer scientific channels rather than pure lobbying.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: A conference-led legitimation strategy is the template other threatened missions will copy to build lawmaker-facing narratives.

insights.claim: NASA's own communications lead frames Roman's oversized cosmic sampling volume as inherently generating vast opportunities for additional science, an institutional argument that wide-field instruments are multi-mission assets by construction.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Wide-field survey hardware amortizes across missions, which is the strongest cost-per-outcome argument for defending big-instrument budgets.
insights.quote: Roman will sample such a large volume of the cosmos that we’ve long known it will offer vast opportunities for a range of additional science,
insights.locator: Those observations could give experts the information

insights.claim: Roman carries a super-wide-angle 300-megapixel infrared camera covering a patch of sky roughly 100 times larger than the Hubble Space Telescope, which is the single specification driving all its secondary capabilities.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: A 100x field-of-view step change turns survey astronomy from targeted observation into bulk inventory — a different cost curve entirely.
insights.locator: Roman, named after NASA’s first chief astronomer

insights.claim: Roman's field of view and infrared vision let it spot asteroids as small as 60 feet long — comparable to the object that exploded over Chelyabinsk in 2013 with the force of 500,000 tons of TNT and sent 1,500 people to hospital.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Detection floor at Chelyabinsk scale is the threshold at which regional-damage events become forecastable rather than surprises.

insights.claim: Roman's asteroid capability requires a software change, not new hardware: the pipeline as designed automatically discards streaks caused by cosmic rays, glitches or asteroids, so astronomers must recover and classify what is currently thrown away.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Capability unlocked by software rather than hardware is nearly free at the margin — the cheapest possible expansion of planetary defense capacity.
insights.quote: Streaks, whether caused by cosmic rays or glitches or asteroids, are caught by the software and discarded,
insights.locator: Roman’s software will need some tweaking

insights.claim: Roman's infrared spectrum gives a decent size estimate plus compositional class — stony, puffy water-rich carbonaceous, or metallic — which in turn constrains density and mass, the inputs needed for both impact-damage estimates and deflection energy budgets.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Composition-to-mass inference is what converts a detection into an actionable mitigation plan; it is the decision-relevant data layer.
insights.quote: This in turn provides strong clues to the composition and thereby the density and mass of the asteroid, which are important when estimating the impact damage or, less ghoulishly, the effort required to nudge it out of its current orbit,
insights.locator: Roman’s infrared scope also allows it

insights.claim: NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office focuses on asteroids 460 feet and larger, of which roughly 25,000 are estimated to be in near-Earth orbits and just over half remain undiscovered.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Half of the catastrophic-class inventory being unfound quantifies an unpriced tail risk and justifies sustained detection funding.

insights.claim: There are an estimated 230,000 near-Earth asteroids around 165 feet long and fewer than 10 percent have been located, each capable of delivering a force comparable to a large atomic bomb without the radiation.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: A 90%+ blind spot in city-damaging objects is the concrete gap that new infrared survey assets are being funded to close.
insights.locator: Astronomers estimate that there are also 230,000

insights.claim: Ground-based telescope networks funded by NASA work well but are fundamentally limited by how much night sky they can cover and by atmospheric interference, which is the structural argument for moving detection to space.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: The physical ceiling on ground assets means detection budget growth flows to spaceborne infrared, not to more mountaintop observatories.
insights.locator: But planetary defenders need to know where they are first

insights.claim: Mitigation options for these objects are limited to kinetic deflection by ramming a spacecraft into them or vaporization possibly using a nuclear weapon, meaning detection lead time is the only variable that can be meaningfully improved today.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: With mitigation fixed, all marginal value in planetary defense accrues to detection and orbit-refinement infrastructure.
insights.locator: These sorts of asteroids could theoretically be deflected

insights.claim: NEO Surveyor launches in 2027 as an explicitly dedicated planetary-defense observatory positioned between Earth and the Sun, using infrared rather than visible light, and could find 90 percent of city-killer-size near-Earth asteroids within a few years.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: A 2027 launch that closes a 90% detection gap in years is the single largest scheduled step-change in planetary defense capability.
insights.locator: That’s why NASA’s launching the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor

insights.claim: The Vera Rubin Observatory has already begun a 10-year survey of the entire night sky from Chile and is expected to discover 89,000 near-Earth asteroids as a byproduct of general cosmic inventorying.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: 89,000 new detections will swamp existing follow-up capacity, making triage tooling the binding constraint rather than discovery.

insights.claim: The operational value of Roman is triage: pointed at a sky corner containing several uncertain objects, it can improve their orbital precision by several orders of magnitude within days, letting scientists rule out most candidates fast.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude orbit refinement in days is the mechanism that converts a flood of alerts into a manageable watchlist.
insights.locator: Here’s how they might all work together

insights.claim: Telescope time is chronically oversubscribed and cannot follow up on every near-Earth asteroid with a non-zero impact probability, so the real scarce resource in planetary defense is follow-up observing capacity rather than detection.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Scarcity sitting in follow-up time means the highest-leverage investment is prioritization capability, not more discovery instruments.
insights.quote: Telescope resources, whether in space or on the ground, are typically oversubscribed and will not be available to follow up on all [near-Earth asteroids] with a non-zero impact probability when they are first discovered,
insights.locator: One, however, might not be able to be ruled out

insights.claim: Roman occupies a different position in space than both NEO Surveyor and the Rubin Observatory, and those parallax differences alone narrow orbital solutions faster than observations from a single vantage point.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Geometric diversity across a distributed sensor fleet is a free accuracy multiplier — an argument for constellation-style planning over single flagship assets.
insights.quote: Those slightly different viewing angles will also help narrow orbits down more quickly than if all objects were looking from the same place,
insights.locator: Roman also occupies a different part of space

insights.claim: JWST already proved the single-target role by playing a key part in tracking 2024 YR4, briefly the most dangerous asteroid ever discovered, but Roman can survey far more asteroids in infrared than JWST could observe in reasonable observing time.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: The division of labor — Roman for breadth, JWST for depth — is the emerging operating model for space-based hazard assessment.
insights.quote: Roman can provide infrared observations of more asteroids than JWST could hope to observe in a reasonable amount of observing time,
